How have you come to your position?
Does you believe that morality is subjective or objective?

We would have to define objective/objectivity first. My personal definition (which I would like to take hold) is that the only truly objective description of a thing can be the actual thing itself - anything else is not perfect, not absolutely precise, has perspective-errors, etc. But there would of course be scales to objectivity, like Newton physics vs. theory of Relativity vs. the yet to achieve fusion of Relativity and Quantum Mechanics vs. who knows what's still left afterwards. So, just because something (e.g. a morality system) might not be truly objective, it could still be almost objective and hence deserve that term in general communication.

Also, what is morality? In my opinion, it can only refer to something that involves at least one living being. Of course I am assuming biological beings, nothing "supernatural" etc. Biological beings would logically be configured by evolution to strive for survival, at least until they have contributed to the perpetuation of their species. Hence I would describe a being as "the living will not to become undone".

Those who understand what evolution is (e.g. that the key aspect is really only the self-replication - everything else follows logically/necessarily) realize that, apart from the chance that created amino acids in the first place (which has e.g. been achieved in the famous Miller-Urey experiment 1952), evolution is an inevitable consequence of the universe. I'm trying to say that evolution is not an arbitrary thing but as objective as the universe itself.

Hence we could also say that a being's will to exist is as objective as the universe itself. But can we hence derive an objective morality that says e.g. "don't act against other beings' existence"? That would be quite a jump. Especially if we take into account how much of a competitive raw heartless nuclear-driven "might makes right"-game evolution really is.

But there's another usually overlooked level: If a being is objectively the will that itself exists, then it is implicitly also the will that the universe exists. The universe, in turn, is the will that the beings can exist. So by extension, a being is the will that other beings can exist, too. I don't know ... could there be a mechanical consequence from this logic that actually played a role in the fact that humans became a rather social species who care for the environment and deem "might makes right" as a generally evil concept?

That's as far as I can take it at the moment.
